title: Barmen (1934)
hookLine: Protestant Christians of the Confessing Church declare that Christ, not Hitler, is Lord
carry: jesus christ is the one word

cards: Swastika flags hang inside some German churches.

A movement calling itself the German Christians wants the Protestant church folded into the new state, a national bishop loyal to Hitler, and pastors of Jewish descent pushed out. Some pastors go along. Others don't.

They gather in a church in Barmen, an industrial town on the Wupper river, Lutherans, Reformed and United side by side, and they write a short statement. It doesn't name Hitler once. It doesn't need to.

teach.h: TO CONFESS: TO SAY IT OUT LOUD.
teach.b: The group that met at Barmen came to be called the Confessing Church, because what they did was confess, in the old sense: say out loud what they believed. The theologian Karl Barth did much of the drafting.

teach.h: A VERSE, A CONFESSION, A REJECTION.
teach.b: The declaration follows a simple pattern: a Bible verse, a statement of faith, then a sentence that says, in effect, we reject the false teaching. The first article opens with the words of Jesus in John.
In the King James Bible: "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me."
Then the line today's carry is drawn from: Jesus Christ, as the Bible bears witness to him, is the one Word of God that the church must hear, trust and obey, in life and in death.
And the rejection: the church may not treat any other event, power, figure or truth as God's revelation alongside him.

Read that in a country where some church voices were hailing the leader as a gift from God, and you hear it without a single name. John's Gospel opens, "In the beginning was the Word," and calls Jesus that Word.

teach.h: ONE WORD, NOT ONE WORD PLUS.
teach.b: Barmen leans on it: one Word, not one Word plus a nation, a race or a leader. Now the honest part. Barmen defended the church's freedom to preach Christ.
It said nothing directly about the Jews being driven from their jobs and homes, and later Christians, including some who were there, came to see that silence as a failure.
Barmen is still read in churches, often by Lutheran and Reformed Christians, as a model of saying no, and as a reminder of what that no left out.

how: Some Lutheran, Reformed and united Protestant churches include the Barmen Declaration among their confessional documents, and it is read and studied in congregations, especially when churches discuss faith and political power.

games.q: you're a pastor, and the new church leaders want loyalty to the state written into your church's teaching. what do you do?
o: go along quietly and keep your pulpit.
meet with others and write down who your Lord is.
games.why: at Barmen, Lutherans and Reformed Christians together wrote that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God the church must obey.

practice: Lord here just means whatever gets the final say. Ask what decides things in your life when it's hard: money, fear, a boss, a belief; notice it without judging, then ask what you'd want to have the final say.
If you pray, say quietly: I am the way, the truth, and the life; if not, name the one thing you won't hand over to anyone.

wordCard.voice: Barmen. The German town where the Confessing Church declared that Jesus Christ alone, and no state or leader, is the Word the church must obey.
